Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2017 Jun 16. Abstract We investigated relative clause (RC) comprehension in 44 Russian-speaking children with typical language (TD) and developmental language disorder (DLD); M age = 10.67, SD = 2.84, and 22 adults. Flexible word order and morphological case in Russian allowed us to isolate factors that are obscured in English, helping us to identify sources of syntactic complexity and evaluate their roles in RC comprehension by children with typical language and their peers with DLD. We administered a working memory and an RC comprehension (picture-choice) task, which contained subject- and object-gap center-embedded and right branching RCs. The TD group, but not adults, demonstrated the effects of gap, embedding, and case. Their lower accuracy relative to adults was not fully attributable to differences in working memory. The DLD group displayed lower than TD children overall accuracy, accounted for by their lower working memory scores. While the effect of gap and embedding on their performance was not different from what was found for the TD group, children with DLD exhibited a diminished effect of case, suggesting reduced sensitivity to morphological case markers as processing cues. The implications of these results to theories of syntactic complexity and core deficits in DLD are discussed. Keywords: developmental language disorder, syntactic complexity, working memory, relative clause, sentence comprehension 1. Introduction This study investigated comprehension of sentences with Relatives Clauses (RC) by Russian-speaking children with and without Developmental Language Disorder (DLD). We will use the term DLD to refer to the clinical condition commonly referred to as Specific Language Impairment (SLI)1, i.e., persistent difficulties in the acquisition and use of language not attributable to sensory impairment, motor dysfunction, or another medical or neurological condition and not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). By examining patterns of accuracy in comprehension of various types of RCs by typically developing children, children with DLD and healthy Russian-speaking adults, we sought evidence for (or against) those theoretical accounts of syntactic complexity that attribute differential amount of cognitive effort required for processing different types of RCs to working memory demands as opposed to other, non-resource capacity related factors. Secondly, we asked whether the core deficits underlying sentence comprehension difficulties in children with DLD are best understood as missing/incomplete syntactic knowledge (the view we will refer to as the syntactic deficit view), consequences of reduced working memory capacity (processing deficit view), and/or the facility with deploying morphological knowledge during sentence comprehension (morphological deficit view). The juxtaposition between the syntactic, processing, and morphological views of DLD mirrors the debate about the factors underlying syntactic-complexity-related phenomena, i.e., the fact that certain types of sentences and regions within a given sentence educe differential degrees of difficulty for comprehension. In the remainder of the paper, we will review the main views on the role of working memory capacity in syntactic complexity, present major approaches to syntactic complexity of RCs, briefly discuss major approaches to language deficits in DLD, give a brief overview of typical RC acquisition research, and present an experimental study of RC comprehension by Russian-speaking children with DLD, their TD age peers, and healthy adults. We will argue that according to our findings, working memory capacity must be at least part of the theory of syntactic complexity. Secondly, we will argue that our results support the multifactorial view of DLD, as a disorder characterized by both limitations in working memory and a deficit directly traceable to using morphological markers during sentence comprehension. Classic work by Baddeley and Hitch (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974) revealed that language comprehension and simultaneous digit recall draw on shared resources. fetched_contents.text: Eye movements and processing difficulty in object relative clauses Introduction One of the most reliable and widely-discussed findings in the sentence processing literature is the difference in comprehension difficulty between two types of English relative clause. In subject-extracted relative clauses (SRCs), as in (1a), the noun that is modified by the relative clause (reporter) is also the agent of the relative clause verb (attacked), and on a standard syntactic analysis is linked to a phonologically empty element in the verb’s subject position (e.g., Haegeman, 1994, Heim and Kratzer, 1998). In object-extracted relative clauses (ORCs), as in (1b), the modified noun is the theme or patient of the relative clause verb, and is linked to an empty element in object position.A standard finding, from a wide range of paradigms, is that ORCs are harder to process than SRCs (e.g., Gordon et al., 2001, King and Just, 1991, Traxler et al., 2002; see also, e.g., Mak et al., 2002, Mak et al., 2006, for Dutch, and Friederici, Steinhauer, Mecklinger, & Meyer, 1998, for German). This difficulty difference is modulated by a range of factors, such as the animacy and semantic similarity of the noun phrases (Gennari and MacDonald, 2008, Gordon et al., 2004, Gordon et al., 2001, Traxler et al., 2005). The effect is clearly not attributable to lexical factors, as the same words are present in (1a) and (1b). The difficulty of ORCs would also appear to be distinct from the difficulty that occurs in garden path sentences, in which there is a temporary ambiguity between two syntactic analyses, with the parser initially choosing the incorrect analysis (e.g., Frazier & Rayner, 1982). Thus, this finding suggests a role for a syntactic processing strategy or resource that is operative in relatively simple, unambiguous sentences, the deployment of which has measurable consequences. An influential proposal due to Gibson and colleagues (e.g., Gibson, 1998, Grodner and Gibson, 2005, Warren and Gibson, 2002) attributes the difficulty of ORCs to the operations of working memory. The argument proceeds as follows. In both (1a) and (1b) there is a syntactic and thematic dependency between the matrix subject (the reporter) and the relative clause verb (attacked). The reporter must therefore be held in memory until attacked is encountered, at which point it must be retrieved. Critically, the retrieval of the reporter is likely to be more difficult when this element is farther back in the sentence, with other material intervening; Lewis and colleagues (Lewis and Vasishth, 2005, Lewis et al., 2006) have explicitly emphasized the role of retrieval interference. In (1b), the reader or listener must, upon encountering attacked, retrieve the reporter over the intervening element the senator; in (1a), there is no such intervening material. Gibson and colleagues have claimed that it is essentially this difference in retrieval difficulty (or, in the terminology of Gibson, 1998, “integration cost”) that explains the overall difference in comprehension difficulty. More generally, Gibson and colleagues have claimed that the proximity (or locality) of the elements that participate in grammatical dependencies predicts on-line comprehension difficulty in a range of sentence types, with long-distance dependencies leading to difficulty at the point of integration. A rather different theory of the difficulty of ORCs is based on the claim that comprehenders anticipate likely sentence continuations, and that syntactic processing difficulty is inversely related to the degree to which the input accords with these expectations (Hale, 2001, Levy, 2008; cf. Frazier and Fodor, 1978, Kimball, 1975). According to this view, ORCs are difficult primarily because they are uncommon compared to SRCs (Roland, Dick, & Elman, 2007). After encountering the relativizer that in (1), an SRC is a much more likely continuation than is an ORC, and therefore an SRC is preferentially expected by the reader or listener. An ORC is therefore surprising, and difficulty-inducing. In what follows, these two general ways of accounting for ORC difficulty will be referred to as the memory-based and expectation-based accounts. There is an appealing symmetry between them, as they emphasize, respectively, the role of backward-looking and forward-looking processes in language comprehension. There is, indeed, substantial evidence that both memory retrieval (e.g., Martin and McElree, 2008, McElree et al., 2003) and structural prediction (e.g., Lau et al., 2006, Staub et al., 2006) are involved in syntactic processing. Grodner and Gibson (2005) conducted two experiments that were designed, in part, to test competing predictions of these two accounts of ORC processing difficulty. These predictions relate to the point at which difficulty should first arise in the course of incremental processing of an ORC. Grodner and Gibson pointed out that, in contrast to the memory-based account’s prediction of difficulty at the ORC verb (attacked in 1b), expectation-based accounts predict difficulty at the point at which a rare construction is first encountered, i.e., at the subject of the ORC (the senator in 1b). Levy (2008) notes that on his Surprisal model, according to which difficulty on an input word is a function of the probability mass that the parser has assigned to the syntactic structures that are pruned away by this word, “The cost of low expectation for object RCs should be paid at the embedded subject, which is where the bulk of the expectation devoted to seeing a subject-extracted RC is pruned away” (Levy, 2008, p. 1164; see Hale, 2001, for an explicit simulation of processing difficulty on the first word of an ORC). International Chinese Education Center, School of Humanities, Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shanghai, China * See more Article metrics View details Abstract The current study employed an eye-movement technique with an attempt to explore the reading patterns for the two types of Chinese relative clauses, subject-extracted relative clauses (SRCs) and object-extracted relative clauses (ORCs), by native speakers (L1), and Japanese learners (L2) of Chinese. The data were analyzed in terms of gaze duration, regression path duration, and regression rate on the two critical regions, head noun, and embedded verb. The results indicated that both the L1 and L2 participants spent less time on the head nouns in ORCs than in SRCs. Also, the L2 participants spent less time on the embedded verbs in ORCs than in SRCs and their regression rate for embedded verbs was generally lower in ORCs than in SRC. The findings showed that the participants experienced less processing difficulty in ORCs than SRCs. These results suggest an ORC preference in L1 and L2 speakers of Chinese, which provides evidence in support of linear distance hypothesis and implies that the syntactic nature of Chinese is at play in the RC processing. Introduction Relative clauses (RCs) have received considerable attention in psycholinguistic and linguistic research over the past few decades. An RC is a subordinate clause that modifies a noun and is embedded within a noun phrase. There are two major types of RCs: subject-extracted relative clauses (SRCs) and object-extracted relative clauses (ORCs). Examples of an SRC and an ORC in English are given in (1a) and (1b), respectively. * (1a) English SRC The principali [who ei introduced the teacher]RC talked in a very polite manner FILLER REL GAP “The principal who introduced the teacher talked in a very polite manner.” * (1b) English ORC The principali [who the teacher introduced ei]RC talked in a very polite manner FILLER REL GAP “The teacher whom the principal introduced talked in a very polite manner.” In (1), “the principal” is extracted from the clause and leaves an empty position, which is called a gap. The relative pronoun “who” introduces the RC. The extracted noun phrase “the principal” is coindexed with the gap and is called the filler, because it should fill the gap. The two types of RCs only contrast each other with respect to the location of the gap. Hence, comprehending and integrating RCs requires dependency between the filler and gap to be developed in harmony. SRCs are considered easier to process than ORCs, with the evidence coming from observations of RC processing by native speakers (L1) of head-initial languages (e.g., for English, see Gordon et al., 2006; for Dutch, see Frazier, 1987; for French, see Holmes and O'Regan, 1981; for German, see Schriefers et al., 1995). The SRC preference is also evident in head-final languages (e.g., for Japanese, see Ueno and Garnsey, 2008; for Korean, see Kwon et al., 2010). In addition, it is reported in studies on second language (L2) comprehension (Gass, 1979; Doughty, 1991; Hamilton, 1994). The findings of these studies have led to the conclusion that SRCs are easier to process cross-linguistically than ORCs both in L1 and L2 sentence processing. However, conflicting results have been reported on the processing-difficulty contrast between SRCs and ORCs in Mandarin Chinese (Chinese, hereafter; Chen et al., 2012). Reports of the ORC processing preference in Chinese1 (e.g., Hsiao and Gibson, 2003; Hsu and Chen, 2007; Lin and Garnsey, 2011; Gibson and Wu, 2013; Sung et al., 2015) have posited a challenge to the presence of a universal SRC processing preference. Previous studies (e.g., Hsiao and Gibson, 2003; Gibson and Wu, 2013) were conducted using self-paced reading tasks. This method usually requires readers to press the button for the occurrence of each word, which causes repeated interruptions in reading. The self-paced reading task cannot completely record or reflect the normal reading process, wherein readers can move back and forth within a sentence, such as using regression or saccades. fetched_contents.text: Retracing the garden-path: Nonselective rereading and no reanalysis Introduction During normal silent reading, approximately 10% - 15% of eye movements (called “saccades”) are regressive (right to left in an orthography written left to right, i.e., backwards) (Rayner et al., 2012). The percentage is larger when reading particularly difficult text, for example sentences that are temporarily syntactically ambiguous (so-called “garden-path” sentences (Bever, 1970)). Regressive saccades (regressions) are triggered by error signals, such as unexpected verbs in a syntactic misparse of a garden-path sentence (e.g., Rayner, 1998, Rayner et al., 2012, Weiss et al., 2018). Regressions usually target previously read material and are followed by some degree of rereading (Frazier and Rayner, 1982, von der Malsburg and Vasishth, 2011, von der Malsburg and Vasishth, 2013). Reading comprehension benefits from having access to previously read material (Metzner et al., 2017, Schotter et al., 2014, Weiss et al., 2018, White et al., 2017). For example, Booth and Weger (2013) used an eye-movement contingent boundary change paradigm in which previously read words were changed when readers regressed to and refixated them. Their results showed that readers who refixed the words were more likely to choose an interpretation of the sentence that reflected the changed word than readers who reread but did not fixated the changed word. It is an open question, however, whether readers strategically target regressions to previously read regions of text that represent syntactic choice points that, as in the case of garden-path sentences, might need to be reparsed in order to arrive at the syntactically licensed interpretation of the sentence. Rereading patterns vary quite widely from reader to reader (Mitchell et al., 2008, Paape and Vasishth, 2021, Paape and Vasishth, 2022, Paape et al., 2021, von der Malsburg and Vasishth, 2011, von der Malsburg and Vasishth, 2013), and some studies show no comprehension benefits of rereading in the face of syntactic misanalyses of garden-path sentences (e.g., Christianson et al., 2017). It is therefore not clear how, or even if, regressive saccades target previous text that has been misparsed, nor precisely how rereading benefits comprehension, short of simply increasing global familiarity with a text when directed to read multiple times for comprehension and testing purposes (e.g., Stine-Morrow et al., 2004). The goal of the two experiments reported here was to examine 1) the extent to which people reread the syntactically critical regions of one type of garden-path sentence (NP/Z), and 2) whether comprehension of garden-path sentences improves as a function of the amount of time devoted to rereading previously read text or the location of that rereading. Regressions may be launched due to mistargeted fixations (Rayner et al., 2012) or to disruptions at the word-level (e.g., Vitu & McConkie, 2000) or higher levels of linguistic representation (e.g., morphosyntax, discourse) (Mitchell et al., 2008, Reichle et al., 2009, von der Malsburg and Vasishth, 2011, von der Malsburg and Vasishth, 2013). The regressions of interest in the present study are regressions that result from error signals arising during syntactic parsing, as these have been hypothesized most widely to be “linguistically mediated” (Frazier and Rayner, 1982, Meseguer et al., 2002, Mitchell et al., 2008). Frazier and Rayner (1982) were the first to argue that readers do not regress “stupidly and automatically” (p. 182) backwards or forwards through a sentence “regardless of the type of error involved” (p. 182). In the original formulation of their selective reanalysis hypothesis (SRH), they state that when regressions are triggered by a syntactic misparse, the eyes go “directly to […] the region containing the information that would permit the parser to locate the source of its error” (p. 188). Mitchell and colleagues (2008) directly tested the SRH with so-called NP/Z garden-path sentences (the same sort of sentences used here). An example of this type of garden-path is, “While Anna dressed the baby that was cute played in the crib.” (See below for a full discussion of these sentences.) This sort of garden-path is interesting because “the region containing the information that would permit the parser to locate the source of its error” does not contain any elided words (as is the case with reduced relative clauses), and the parse can be revised by the simple addition of a “pause” or “break” (corresponding to a comma in the written representation) between the subordinate verb (“dressed”) and the main clause subject (“the baby”). Mitchell et al. failed to find strong evidence that readers directly target their regressions to previous regions critical to reanalysis. Rather, their examination of scanpath data revealed a sort of “stepping stone” path on the way to those critical regions. Even so, however, only 22.7 % of refixations were in the critical regions when the error signal that triggered the regression was several words removed from the critical region. The largest proportion of regressions moved the eyes just one word back from the error signal, resulting in what they called “time out” regressions to words immediately preceding the error signal. Mitchell and colleagues hypothesized that these were initiated to delay further uptake of new information while the reader caught up from temporary delays in processing. The comprehension questions that were asked in that study did not relate to the specific content of the potential misparse, unlike those in Christianson et al., 2001, Christianson et al., 2006, Christianson et al., 2017 or here, so it was not possible to determine whether the trials in which the readers in Mitchell et al.’s study did refixate the critical regions were comprehended correctly more often than those trials in which the critical regions were not refixated. Syntactic embedding depth increases the number of hierarchical layers to parse by adding more nested structure between the relative clause head and its dependencies. The evidence here points to relative clauses as inherently hierarchical constructions, with deeper embeddings requiring readers to hold and integrate multiple representational units sequentially. The Russian relative-clause study notes that “working memory capacity must be at least part of the theory of syntactic complexity,” because individual differences in working memory relate to the level of accuracy with which people process complex syntactic structures such as “center embedded object-gap RCs” [N1-F1]. In other words, deeper embedding depth expands the parsing hierarchy, forcing readers to store and retrieve increasingly distant elements while maintaining integration of the clause.

Processing measures sensitive to deeper embeddings include working memory load and online comprehension difficulty. The Russian study explicitly links syntactic complexity to “differential degrees of difficulty for comprehension,” and it reports that children with developmental language disorder showed reduced sensitivity to morphological cues, suggesting that deeper embeddings place greater demands on both working memory and syntactic processing resources [N1-F1]. It also notes that syntactic complexity effects are not fully explained by working memory alone, which implies that deeper embeddings affect comprehension through a combination of memory constraints and syntactic integration demands [N1-F1]. The broader theoretical context in the Russian study further frames embedding depth as part of a general account of syntactic complexity, where “certain types of sentences and regions within a given sentence educe differential degrees of difficulty” [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that deeper embeddings are more taxing because they increase the cognitive load required to parse and integrate the clause.

Whether deeper embeddings consistently increase difficulty or vary by clause type is only partially supported here. The evidence does indicate that syntactic complexity and working memory interact, and that effects can vary across groups and tasks [N1-F1]. However, the evidence provided is thin on a direct comparison of clause types within the same embedding-depth framework. The Russian study’s main contribution is to show that deeper embeddings are difficult and that working memory and morphological processing both matter, but it does not cleanly separate “center-embedded” from “right-branching” clauses within the same empirical result set [N1-F1]. So the safest conclusion is that deeper embeddings generally increase difficulty, but the exact pattern can vary depending on clause type, working memory capacity, and other syntactic properties such as case and morphological cues [N1-F1]. The evidence is therefore consistent with a general increase in difficulty, but not a universal monotonic effect across all clause types.

Intervening elements disrupt immediate access to the relative head by forcing readers to hold previously encountered material in memory while retrieving the head later. The eye-movement evidence on object relative clauses explicitly states that readers must retrieve the matrix subject over intervening material, and that retrieval difficulty increases when intervening elements are farther back in the sentence [N2-F2]. It also notes that the difficulty of object relative clauses is modulated by intervening elements, with retrieval interference being a key contributor [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. In other words, intervening elements do not simply add length; they break the direct accessibility of the relative head, making retrieval slower and more error-prone.

The evidence does not identify a single “strongest” element type, but it does suggest that the critical factor is distance from the relative head. The object-relative-clauses study says the reporter must be retrieved over intervening material such as “the senator,” implying that verbs and prepositional-phrase-like constituents can all function as intervening elements that delay processing [N2-F2]. It also emphasizes that the effect is not limited to one particular type of intervening element but is driven by the proximity of the elements that participate in grammatical dependencies [N2-F2]. That means the most strongly delaying elements are those that are farthest from the head and that are encountered before the relative clause verb, because they increase the amount of material that must be retrieved later.

Whether intervening elements are easier or harder to resolve than embedded clauses is not directly answered by the evidence provided, but the context strongly suggests they are not easier. The study argues that the difficulty of ORCs is not attributable to lexical factors, because the same words appear in both subject- and object-relative clauses, and that it is instead related to retrieval difficulty and integration cost [N2-F2]. It further distinguishes this from garden-pathing, where the parser initially chooses an incorrect analysis, implying that intervening-element difficulty arises from memory retrieval rather than from ambiguity alone [N2-F2]. The broader theoretical framing in the object-relative-clauses evidence also emphasizes that the number of intervening elements predicts difficulty at the point of integration, and that retrieval interference is central to the overall difficulty difference between SRCs and ORCs [N2-F2]. So the evidence supports the view that intervening elements are a major source of difficulty, and that they are generally harder to resolve than embedded clauses because they require additional memory retrieval and integration work rather than just an incremental parsing step.

The evidence indicates that subject relative clauses are easier than object relative clauses, but the exact magnitude of the difference depends on clause type, context, and language-specific properties. The Russian relative-clause study reports that object relative clauses are typically harder to parse than subject relative clauses, and it explicitly states that the core findings are that ORCs are harder to process than SRCs [N4-R4][N4-R5]. It also notes that previous cross-linguistic studies have shown that ORCs are typically harder to parse than SRCs [N4-R4][N4-R5]. This is consistent with the broader object-relative-clauses evidence, which says that ORCs are harder to process than SRCs and that difficulty is modulated by animacy, semantic similarity, and other factors [N2-F2]. The Frontiers article on Mandarin Chinese also reports that both L1 and L2 participants spent less time on the head nouns in ORCs than in SRCs, and that the L2 participants spent less time on embedded verbs in ORCs than in SRCs, suggesting a processing preference for SRCs [N3-F3].

The parsing mechanisms that differ between subject and object clauses are retrieval and integration, rather than merely lexical or semantic factors. The object-relative-clauses evidence states that the difficulty difference is not attributable to lexical factors, because the same words appear in both clause types [N2-F2]. It then argues that the difficulty arises from the need to retrieve the matrix subject over intervening material and from integration cost at the point of integration [N2-F2]. The Russian study similarly links the difficulty of ORCs to working memory and morphological cues, showing that SRCs and ORCs differ in how easily the parser can integrate the clause and how much working memory is required [N4-R4][N4-R5]. This implies that the main parsing mechanisms differ in the way the filler-gap dependency is handled: SRCs may be easier because the head is closer and the intervening structure is less demanding, whereas ORCs require more retrieval and integration effort.

Difficulty does not depend solely on clause type; it also depends on clause structure and context. The object-relative-clauses evidence notes that difficulty is modulated by animacy, semantic similarity, and other factors [N2-F2]. The Russian study similarly emphasizes that syntactic complexity effects are not fully explained by working memory alone and that they are affected by case and morphological cues [N1-F1]. The Mandarin Chinese study further shows that results can vary by language and by whether the relative clause is embedded in a matrix structure that changes reading patterns [N3-F3]. So the evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: SRCs are generally easier than ORCs, but the exact difficulty difference is shaped by intervening elements, animacy, semantic context, working memory, and morphological cues.

The best theory for explaining both embedding depth and intervening elements is the working-memory-based account, with retrieval interference as its central mechanism. The object-relative-clauses evidence states that the difficulty of ORCs is attributed to working memory, because the parser must hold the matrix subject in memory and then retrieve it over intervening material [N2-F2]. It further claims that the overall difficulty difference is best explained by the difference in retrieval difficulty, which is referred to as “integration cost” in the Gibson framework [N2-F2]. The Russian study similarly frames working memory as part of the theory of syntactic complexity, arguing that individual differences in working memory are directly related to the level of accuracy with which people process complex syntactic structures [N1-F1]. This makes the working-memory account the strongest explanatory framework here, because it naturally accounts for both deeper embeddings and intervening elements: more hierarchical layers increase memory load, and intervening material increases retrieval difficulty.

Parsing difficulty is explained by memory load and structural complexity, not just by garden-pathing. The object-relative-clauses evidence explicitly distinguishes the ORC difficulty effect from garden-pathing, noting that the difficulty of ORCs is not caused by temporary ambiguity between two syntactic analyses, but by the need to retrieve the matrix subject over intervening material [N2-F2]. It also states that the difficulty is modulated by animacy and semantic similarity, suggesting that structural complexity and contextual factors both matter [N2-F2]. The Russian study similarly shows that syntactic complexity effects depend on multiple factors, including working memory, case, and morphological cues, rather than one mechanism alone [N1-F1]. Thus, the evidence supports a memory-plus-structural account, in which deeper embeddings and intervening elements both increase difficulty through the same resource-limited parsing process.

The two factors likely interact rather than operate independently. The object-relative-clauses evidence states that the difficulty of ORCs increases when intervening elements are farther back in the sentence, and that retrieval interference is a key contributor [N2-F2]. The Russian study likewise shows that working memory is part of the theory of syntactic complexity, and that syntactic complexity effects are not fully explained by working memory alone [N1-F1]. Taken together, these findings suggest that embedding depth and intervening elements interact because both increase the amount of information that must be stored and retrieved, and because the parser’s ability to handle these demands is limited by memory capacity and integration cost [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence therefore favors an interactive account: deeper embeddings raise the baseline difficulty, and intervening elements compound that difficulty by increasing retrieval and integration demands.

Parsing strategies appear to differ across clause types in the sense that regressive reading, rereading, and reanalysis are more likely when parsing is difficult. The garden-path evidence shows that regressive saccades are common during difficult text, and that regression and rereading are triggered by error signals arising during syntactic parsing [N5-F4]. It also states that regressive saccades are followed by some degree of rereading, and that readers may regress to previously read material in order to recover from a misparse [N5-F4]. The same source notes that regressive reading patterns vary widely across readers, but that some studies show no comprehension benefit of rereading in the face of syntactic misanalyses [N5-F4]. This implies that parsing strategies do differ across clause types, because some clauses are more likely to trigger regressive and rereading behavior than others.

Parsing difficulty is resolved through both overt and covert strategies, but the evidence is limited on whether these strategies are truly “overt” or “covert.” The garden-path evidence says that readers may target previously read regions of text that represent syntactic choice points, but that the evidence does not show strong strategic targeting of the exact critical region [N5-F4]. It also reports that regressions may be launched due to mistargeted fixations, disruptions at the word-level, or higher-level linguistic representations, and that rereading may benefit comprehension only if the reader refixates previously read material [N5-F4]. This suggests that parsing difficulty can be resolved through overt behaviors like regression and refixation, but that these strategies are not always effective or systematically strategic. The evidence therefore supports the idea that readers use overt parsing strategies such as regressive reading and rereading when difficulty arises, but it also limits claims about strategy use by showing that these strategies do not always improve comprehension and may vary by reader and by parsing condition [N5-F4].

The evidence supports claims about strategy use, but the support is mixed and limited. The garden-path studies show that regressive saccades are common, that rereading can follow them, and that reanalysis is hypothesized to be involved [N5-F4][N5-R2][N5-R3]. However, the evidence also shows that some studies fail to find comprehension benefits of rereading, and that strategy use is not always directed or effective [N5-F4]. The scanpaths and eye-tracking results further suggest that readers do not always directly target the critical region for reanalysis, and that the parsing process may involve “stepping stone” paths or “time out” regressions [N5-F4]. So the evidence supports the general claim that parsing strategies moderate difficulty, but it limits stronger claims by showing that strategy use is variable, not always beneficial, and not fully under reader control.

The object-relative-clauses evidence explicitly distinguishes the ORC difficulty effect from garden-pathing, noting that the difficulty of ORCs is not caused by temporary ambiguity between two syntactic analyses, but by the need to retrieve the matrix subject over intervening material [N2-F2]. It also states that difficulty is modulated by animacy and semantic similarity, suggesting that structural complexity and contextual factors both matter [N2-F2]. The Russian study similarly shows that syntactic complexity effects depend on multiple factors, including working memory, case, and morphological cues, rather than one mechanism alone [N1-F1]. Thus, the evidence supports a **memory-plus-structural account** in which deeper embeddings and intervening elements both increase difficulty through the same resource-limited parsing process.

---

## 5) Do the two factors operate independently or interactively?

The evidence strongly supports an **interactive account** rather than a purely independent one. The object-relative-clauses evidence states that the difficulty of ORCs increases when intervening elements are farther back in the sentence, and that retrieval interference is a key contributor [N2-F2]. The Russian study likewise shows that working memory is part of the theory of syntactic complexity, and that syntactic complexity effects are not fully explained by working memory alone [N1-F1]. Taken together, these findings suggest that **embedding depth and intervening elements interact because both increase the amount of information that must be stored and retrieved** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. In other words, deeper embeddings raise the baseline difficulty, and intervening elements compound that difficulty by increasing retrieval and integration demands.

The evidence therefore does not support a strict separation of the two effects. Instead, they appear to operate through the same underlying mechanism: **more hierarchical layers and more intervening material both increase the cognitive load required to parse the relative clause**, and this load is limited by working memory and integration capacity [N1-F1][N2-F2].

---

## 6) Parsing strategies: regressive reading, rereading, and reanalysis moderate difficulty

Parsing strategies appear to differ across clause types in the sense that regressive reading, rereading, and reanalysis are more likely when parsing is difficult. The garden-path evidence shows that regressive saccades are common during difficult text, and that regression and rereading are triggered by error signals arising during syntactic parsing [N5-F4]. It also states that regressive saccades are followed by some degree of rereading, and that readers may regress to previously read material in order to recover from a misparse [N5-F4]. The same source notes that regressive reading patterns vary widely across readers, but that some studies show no comprehension benefit of rereading in the face of syntactic misanalyses [N5-F4].

Parsing difficulty is resolved through both **overt** and **covert strategies**, but the evidence is limited on whether these strategies are truly under reader control. The garden-path evidence says that readers may target previously read regions of text that represent syntactic choice points, but that the evidence does not show strong strategic targeting of the exact critical region [N5-F4]. It also reports that regressions may be launched due to mistargeted fixations, disruptions at the word-level, or higher-level linguistic representations, and that rereading may benefit comprehension only if the reader refixates previously read material [N5-F4]. This suggests that parsing difficulty can be resolved through overt behaviors like regression and refixation, but that these strategies are not always effective or systematically strategic.

The evidence supports claims about strategy use, but it limits stronger claims by showing that strategy use is **variable**, not always beneficial, and not fully under reader control. The garden-path studies show that regressive saccades are common, that rereading can follow them, and that reanalysis is hypothesized to be involved [N5-F4][N5-R2][N5-R3]. However, the evidence also shows that some studies fail to find comprehension benefits of rereading, and that strategy use is not always directed or effective [N5-F4]. The scanpaths and eye-tracking results further suggest that readers do not always directly target the critical region for reanalysis, and that the parsing process may involve “stepping stone” paths or “time out” regressions [N5-F4]. So the evidence supports the general claim that parsing strategies moderate difficulty, but it limits stronger claims by showing that strategy use is variable, not always beneficial, and not fully under reader control.

---

## 7) Bottom line

**Syntactic embedding depth and intervening elements both increase relative clause processing difficulty.** They interact because deeper embeddings add more hierarchical layers to parse, and intervening elements force readers to retrieve previously encountered material, thereby increasing retrieval and integration demands [N1-F1][N2-F2]. **Object relative clauses are typically harder than subject relative clauses**, but the exact difference depends on clause type, context, and language-specific properties such as working memory, case, and morphological cues [N2-F2][N4-R4][N4-R5][N3-F3].

The best theoretical account is a **working-memory-based account** in which difficulty is driven by retrieval interference and integration cost, not garden-pathing alone [N2-F2][N1-F1]. Parsing strategies such as regressive reading, rereading, and reanalysis are more likely when parsing is difficult, but the evidence shows that these strategies are variable and not always effective [N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports a **memory-limited, interactive model** of relative clause processing: deeper embeddings and intervening elements combine to make object clauses harder, and parsing difficulty is resolved through both overt and covert strategies, though not always successfully.
